title: Cell: The Building Block of Life

topics.title: Discovery of cells and the cell theory

learn.hook: A thin slice of cork looked like a honeycomb of tiny empty rooms under a microscope. That simple look in 1665 began the whole science of cells!
points: In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork through his microscope, saw small box-like compartments and named them 'cells'.
In 1674 Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, using better lenses, was the first to see free-living cells in pond water.
In 1831 Robert Brown discovered the nucleus in plant cells.
Schleiden (1838, plants) and Schwann (1839, animals) proposed the cell theory: all plants and animals are made of cells, and the cell is the basic unit of life.
In 1855 Rudolf Virchow added that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

example.q: Think it through: Hooke's cork cells looked empty, like little rooms with walls. Why?
steps: Cork comes from the bark of a tree.
Cork cells are dead cells.
When a cell dies, its living contents are lost but its cell wall remains.
So Hooke saw only the walls of the cells.
example.answer: Cork cells are dead, so only their cell walls were left to see.

learn.reallife: Every pathology lab that checks a blood sample or a biopsy under a microscope builds on the cell theory.

games.title: Cell discovery timeline
games.prompt: Arrange these discoveries from earliest to latest
items: Leeuwenhoek sees living cells in pond water (1674)
Schleiden: plants are made of cells (1838)
Schwann: animals are made of cells (1839)
Virchow: cells come from pre-existing cells (1855)

games.title: Cell theory: true or false?
items: All living organisms are made of one or more cells
This is the first idea of the cell theory.
The cork cells Hooke saw were living cells
Cork cells are dead. Hooke saw only their cell walls.
New cells arise from cells that already exist
Brown described the nucleus in plant cells in 1831.
The cell theory was proposed by a single scientist working alone
It grew from the work of Schleiden and Schwann, and Virchow later added to it.

quiz.q: Who first observed and named 'cells' while looking at a thin slice of cork?
quiz.explain: Robert Hooke saw box-like compartments in cork in 1665 and called them cells.
steps: Asked: who first saw and named cells in cork.
Fact: in 1665 Robert Hooke saw box-like compartments in cork and called them cells.
Brown found the nucleus; Virchow and Schwann came later.
Answer: Robert Hooke
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Robert Hooke with Robert Brown, who discovered the nucleus

quiz.q: In which year did Robert Hooke observe cells in cork?
quiz.explain: Hooke published his observations of cork cells in 1665 in his book Micrographia.
steps: Timeline: Hooke 1665, Leeuwenhoek 1674, Brown 1831, Virchow 1855.
Hooke's cork observation was in 1665.
Answer: 1665
quiz.mistake: Confuses the dates of different cell discoveries

quiz.q: Who was the first to see free-living cells in pond water?
quiz.explain: In 1674 Leeuwenhoek used his improved lenses to see tiny living cells moving in pond water.
steps: Hooke saw dead cork cells, not free-living ones.
In 1674 Leeuwenhoek, with better lenses, saw free-living cells in pond water.
Answer: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
quiz.mistake: Thinks Hooke saw living cells, but Hooke saw dead cork cells

quiz.q: Which scientist stated that all cells arise from pre-existing cells?
quiz.explain: Rudolf Virchow added this idea to the cell theory in 1855.
steps: Schleiden and Schwann: all plants and animals are made of cells.
In 1855 Virchow added: all cells arise from pre-existing cells.
Answer: Rudolf Virchow
quiz.mistake: Does not know which scientist added the third idea of the cell theory

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a part of the cell theory?
options: All living organisms are made of cells
The cell is the basic unit of life
All cells have a cell wall
All cells arise from pre-existing cells
quiz.explain: Animal cells have no cell wall, so this cannot be a rule for all cells. The other three are the ideas of the cell theory.
steps: Cell theory: organisms are made of cells; the cell is the basic unit; cells arise from pre-existing cells.
Animal cells have no cell wall.
So 'All cells have a cell wall' is NOT part of the cell theory.
Answer: All cells have a cell wall
quiz.mistake: Thinks every cell has a cell wall, like plant cells

quiz.q: What did Robert Brown discover in 1831?
quiz.explain: Robert Brown observed and described the nucleus in plant cells.
steps: Timeline: Brown, 1831.
He discovered the nucleus in plant cells.
Answer: The nucleus
quiz.mistake: Confuses the discovery of the nucleus with the discovery of the cell

quiz.q: Schleiden studied plants and Schwann studied animals. What did their combined work show?
options: Plants and animals are made of cells
Only plants are made of cells
Cells can form from non-living matter
Animals have bigger cells than plants
quiz.explain: Together they showed that both plants and animals are built from cells, which became the cell theory.
steps: Schleiden (1838) studied plants; Schwann (1839) studied animals.
Together: all plants and animals are made of cells.
Answer: Plants and animals are made of cells
quiz.mistake: Thinks the cell theory was only about plants

quiz.q: Why are microscopes needed to study most cells?
options: Cells are invisible because they are transparent gas
Cells glow only under a lens
Most cells are too small to be seen with the naked eye
quiz.explain: Most cells are only a few micrometres across, far smaller than the eye can see, so a lens is needed to magnify them.
steps: Most cells are far smaller than the naked eye can see.
A microscope magnifies them.
Answer: Most cells are too small to be seen with the naked eye
quiz.mistake: Does not understand how tiny most cells are

teach.ask: Gappu peers at an onion peel: "My teacher says I am made of cells too. What is this cell theory everyone talks about?"
teach.praise: Chirp! All living things are made of cells, the cell is the basic unit of life, and new cells come only from old cells. I am a bird made of billions of cells!
teach.nudge: And where do new cells come from? Do they just appear out of nothing?

revise.summary: Hooke named cells in cork in 1665, Leeuwenhoek saw living cells in 1674, and Brown found the nucleus in 1831. Schleiden and Schwann's cell theory, extended by Virchow, says all organisms are made of cells, which arise from pre-existing cells.
focus: Discoveries and dates: Hooke, Leeuwenhoek, Brown, Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow
The points of the cell theory
Why Hooke's cork cells looked empty
remember: 1855 Virchow: all cells arise from pre-existing cells
traps: 'All cells have a cell wall' is not part of the cell theory
Hooke saw dead cork cells; Leeuwenhoek first saw living cells
Don't credit Virchow with discovering the nucleus

learn.hook: A cell is like a busy little city: it has a control room, power stations, factories, a packing office and even a recycling unit!
points: The cell membrane is selectively permeable: it lets some substances in and out and stops others. Plant cells also have a tough outer cell wall made mainly of cellulose.
The nucleus has a double membrane and contains chromosomes made of DNA. It controls the cell's activities and carries information passed on to new cells.
Mitochondria release energy from food in the form of ATP, so they are called the powerhouses of the cell. Ribosomes make proteins.

Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of channels: rough ER has ribosomes and helps make proteins; smooth ER helps make fats (lipids). The Golgi apparatus packages materials and sends them to where they are needed.
Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes and are called 'suicide bags'. Plastids (such as chloroplasts with green chlorophyll) and a large central vacuole are found in plant cells.

example.q: Think it through: Dry kishmish (raisins) are soaked in water overnight. In the morning they are plump. What happened?
steps: The inside of a raisin has a lot of sugar and very little water.
The cell membranes of the raisin are selectively permeable.
Water moves through them from where there is more water (outside) to where there is less water (inside).
This movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane is osmosis, so the raisins swell.
example.answer: Water entered the raisin cells by osmosis, so the raisins swelled.

learn.reallife: Salt on cucumber slices pulls water out of the cells by osmosis, which is why salted kheera becomes watery and limp.

games.title: Match the organelle to its job
pairs: Controls the activities of the cell

quiz.q: Which organelle is called the powerhouse of the cell?
quiz.explain: Mitochondria release energy from food and store it as ATP, the energy currency of the cell.
steps: Mitochondria release energy from food as ATP.
So they are called the powerhouses of the cell.
Answer: Mitochondrion
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the organelle that makes proteins with the one that releases energy

quiz.q: Which organelle packages materials made in the cell and sends them to their destinations?
quiz.explain: The Golgi apparatus modifies, packs and dispatches materials, many of which come from the ER.
steps: The Golgi apparatus packages materials and sends them where needed.
Answer: Golgi apparatus
quiz.mistake: Confuses packaging with making or storing materials

quiz.q: Lysosomes are called 'suicide bags'. Why?
options: If the cell is damaged they can burst and their enzymes digest the cell
They make proteins for the cell
quiz.explain: Lysosomes are full of powerful digestive enzymes. When a cell is badly damaged, they may burst and digest their own cell.
steps: Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes.
If the cell is damaged they can burst and digest the cell itself.
Hence 'suicide bags'.
Answer: If the cell is damaged they can burst and their enzymes digest the cell
quiz.mistake: Does not link lysosomes with digestive enzymes

quiz.q: Where in the cell are proteins made?
quiz.explain: Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis. Many are attached to rough ER.
steps: Ribosomes make proteins (many sit on rough ER).
Answer: Ribosomes
quiz.mistake: Thinks storage organelles also make proteins

quiz.q: Which part of the cell allows some substances to pass but stops others?
quiz.explain: The cell membrane is selectively permeable. It controls what enters and leaves the cell.
steps: The cell membrane is selectively permeable.
It lets some substances in and out and stops others.
Answer: The cell membrane
quiz.mistake: Thinks the cell wall controls entry; the cell wall is freely permeable

quiz.q: The cell wall of a plant cell is mainly made of
quiz.explain: Plant cell walls are made mostly of cellulose, which gives strength and shape. Chitin is found in fungal cell walls.
steps: The plant cell wall is made mainly of cellulose.
Chitin is in fungal walls.
Answer: cellulose
quiz.mistake: Confuses the plant cell wall with the fungal cell wall

quiz.q: Slices of cucumber sprinkled with salt become watery after some time. Why?
options: Water moves out of the cucumber cells by osmosis
The cucumber cells absorb the salt and burst
quiz.explain: The salty layer outside has less water than the cells, so water moves out of the cells across their membranes by osmosis.
steps: Salt outside makes the outer solution less watery than the cell contents.
Water moves out of the cells through their membranes by osmosis.
So the slices become watery.
Answer: Water moves out of the cucumber cells by osmosis
quiz.mistake: Thinks water moves towards where there is more water, not less

quiz.q: Why are the cells of a spinach leaf green?
options: They contain chloroplasts with the pigment chlorophyll
quiz.explain: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, a green pigment that traps sunlight for photosynthesis.
steps: Plastids called chloroplasts contain green chlorophyll.
Spinach leaf cells have many chloroplasts.
Answer: They contain chloroplasts with the pigment chlorophyll
quiz.mistake: Thinks the colour comes from the cell wall or the nucleus

teach.ask: Gappu imagines shrinking into a cell: "Who is the boss in there, and who makes the energy? Tell me about the parts!"
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! The nucleus controls, mitochondria give energy, the membrane guards the gate and every other organelle has its own job. What a busy city!
teach.nudge: But how does the cell decide what can come inside and what must stay out?

revise.summary: Each organelle has a job: the membrane controls entry, the nucleus controls the cell, mitochondria release energy, ribosomes make proteins, ER and Golgi make and dispatch materials, lysosomes digest, and plant cells have walls, plastids and big vacuoles.
focus: Functions of membrane, wall, nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, plastids, vacuole
Organelles found only in plant cells
remember: Rough ER (ribosomes) → proteins; smooth ER → lipids
Plant cell wall = cellulose; chloroplasts contain chlorophyll
traps: The cell wall is not selectively permeable like the membrane
Plant walls are cellulose, not chitin
Water moves out of cells in salt by osmosis; salt does not create water

learn.hook: An Amoeba is just one cell, yet it eats, moves, breathes and divides. You are trillions of cells working as a team. Both are alive!
points: Unicellular organisms are made of a single cell that carries out all life processes. Examples: Amoeba, Paramecium, Chlamydomonas, yeast and bacteria.
Multicellular organisms are made of many cells. Examples: Hydra, mango trees, mushrooms, earthworms and humans.
In multicellular organisms cells are specialised for different jobs, called division of labour. Nerve cells carry messages and red blood cells carry oxygen.
Cells differ in shape and size according to their job. Amoeba changes shape using pseudopodia, while nerve cells are long and branched.
Prokaryotic cells (such as bacteria) have no nuclear membrane and no membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotic cells (plants, animals, fungi, Amoeba) have a true nucleus with a nuclear membrane.

example.q: Think it through: Why can a single-celled Paramecium survive on its own, while a single cell taken from your liver cannot live alone in a pond?
steps: A Paramecium's single cell does everything: taking in food, getting energy, removing waste and reproducing.
A liver cell is specialised for a few jobs only.
It depends on other cells, such as blood cells that bring it food and oxygen.
On its own it cannot carry out every life process.
example.answer: Paramecium's one cell performs all life processes, but a specialised liver cell depends on other cells.

learn.reallife: The yeast that makes idli and dosa batter rise and the bacteria that set milk into curd are unicellular helpers in every Indian kitchen.

items.text: Bacteria have ___ cells, with no nuclear membrane.
Amoeba moves and catches food using finger-like ___.
Specialised cells sharing different jobs in a body is called division of ___.
Plant and animal cells have a true nucleus, so they are ___ cells.
Nerve cells are long and branched because they carry ___.

quiz.q: Which of these organisms is unicellular?
quiz.explain: Amoeba is made of just one cell that carries out all life processes. The others are multicellular.
steps: Unicellular examples: Amoeba, Paramecium, Chlamydomonas, yeast, bacteria.
Earthworm, Hydra and mushroom are multicellular.
Answer: Amoeba
quiz.mistake: Thinks every tiny organism, like Hydra, must be unicellular

quiz.q: Which of these is a multicellular organism?
quiz.explain: Hydra is a small animal made of many cells. Paramecium, Chlamydomonas and yeast are single-celled.
steps: Multicellular examples: Hydra, mango trees, mushrooms, earthworms, humans.
Paramecium, Chlamydomonas and yeast are unicellular.
Answer: Hydra
quiz.mistake: Judges whether something is unicellular only by how small it is

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of cells being specialised in a multicellular organism?
options: Different jobs are shared, so the body works efficiently
quiz.explain: Division of labour lets each type of cell do its job very well, such as muscle cells contracting and nerve cells carrying messages.
steps: In multicellular organisms cells are specialised: division of labour.
Each cell type does its job well, so the body works efficiently.
Answer: Different jobs are shared, so the body works efficiently
quiz.mistake: Thinks specialisation makes cells independent rather than dependent on each other

quiz.q: What does a prokaryotic cell lack?
quiz.explain: In prokaryotes the genetic material lies in the cytoplasm without a nuclear membrane. They do have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes.
steps: Prokaryotic cells have no nuclear membrane and no membrane-bound organelles.
They still have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes.
Answer: A nuclear membrane
quiz.mistake: Thinks prokaryotes lack all cell parts, including ribosomes

quiz.q: Which organism has prokaryotic cells?
quiz.explain: Bacteria are prokaryotes. Amoeba and yeast are single-celled but eukaryotic, with a true nucleus.
steps: Bacteria are prokaryotes.
Amoeba, yeast and mango trees are eukaryotic.
Answer: Bacteria
quiz.mistake: Thinks every unicellular organism is prokaryotic

quiz.q: In a unicellular organism, who performs life processes such as feeding, respiration and excretion?
options: Nobody; they do not need them
quiz.explain: A unicellular organism has only one cell, so that one cell must do every life process.
steps: A unicellular organism has only one cell.
That single cell carries out all life processes.
Answer: The single cell itself
quiz.mistake: Thinks life processes need organs, so single cells cannot have them

quiz.q: Which organism changes its shape and moves using pseudopodia?
quiz.explain: Amoeba pushes out finger-like pseudopodia to move and to capture food. Paramecium moves using tiny hair-like cilia.
steps: Amoeba changes shape using pseudopodia.
Paramecium uses cilia.
Answer: Amoeba
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the ways Amoeba and Paramecium move

quiz.q: Which of these is a eukaryotic cell?
quiz.explain: Onion cells, like all plant cells, have a true nucleus with a nuclear membrane. Bacteria and cyanobacteria are prokaryotes.
steps: Eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus with a nuclear membrane.
Plant cells such as onion peel cells are eukaryotic.
Bacteria and cyanobacteria are prokaryotes. Answer: An onion peel cell
quiz.mistake: Does not know that cyanobacteria are bacteria, so prokaryotic

teach.ask: Gappu blinks: "An Amoeba is only ONE cell, and I am made of billions. How can both of us be alive?"
teach.praise: Chirp! An Amoeba's one cell does every job by itself, while my many cells share the work through division of labour. We are both alive!
teach.nudge: So in my body, does every cell do every job, or do they share the work?

revise.summary: Unicellular organisms do all life processes in one cell; multicellular organisms have specialised cells sharing jobs. Prokaryotes like bacteria lack a nuclear membrane, while eukaryotes have a true nucleus.
focus: Examples of unicellular and multicellular organisms
Division of labour and cell shape linked to job
remember: Unicellular: Amoeba, Paramecium, Chlamydomonas, yeast, bacteria
Multicellular: Hydra, mango tree, mushroom, earthworm, humans
Prokaryote = no nuclear membrane, no membrane-bound organelles
Amoeba moves by pseudopodia; Paramecium by cilia
traps: Yeast and Amoeba are unicellular but eukaryotic
Prokaryotes still have a cell membrane and ribosomes
A specialised cell cannot live alone like a unicellular organism
